Purity and Formulations.intro: In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one element or compound. Formulations are mixtures carefully designed for specific purposes.

sections.title: Pure Substances
points: Contains only one type of element or compound — no other substances
Has a sharp, specific melting and boiling point
Impurities lower the melting point and broaden the melting range
Melting point test: pure substance melts at exact temperature; impure melts over a range

sections.title: Formulations
points: A formulation is a useful mixture with precise proportions of each component
Each component has a specific purpose
Examples: medicines (precise drug dose + inactive ingredients), fuels (additives for performance), cleaning products, alloys, paints, fertilisers, foods

keyTerms.def: A substance containing only one type of element or compound; has a sharp melting point
A mixture designed with precise proportions for a specific purpose
The temperature at which a substance changes from solid to liquid

examTips: Pure = sharp melting point. Impure = lower and broader melting range.
Formulations are NOT pure — they are deliberately designed mixtures.
commonMistakes: Saying pure water is a formulation — it is a pure compound.
Forgetting that impurities lower (not raise) the melting point.

Chromatography.intro: Chromatography separates mixtures based on how strongly each component interacts with the stationary and mobile phases. It is used to identify substances.

sections.title: How Chromatography Works
points: Mobile phase: solvent that travels through the stationary phase
Stationary phase: paper (or other medium) that doesn't move
Each substance moves different distances depending on: solubility in solvent AND attraction to paper
More soluble / less attracted to paper → moves further up

callout.label: Rf Formula
callout.text: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front. Rf is always between 0 and 1. Same Rf in same solvent = possibly same substance.

sections.title: Interpreting Results
points: One spot = pure substance (or only one component present)
Multiple spots = mixture
Compare Rf values with known substances to identify unknowns
Use multiple solvents to confirm identity — same Rf in different solvents = likely same substance

keyTerms.def: Ratio of distance moved by substance to distance moved by solvent — always 0 to 1
The solvent that carries substances through the stationary phase
The paper or other medium that does not move
Technique that separates mixtures based on different affinities for mobile and stationary phases

examTips: Rf = substance distance ÷ solvent distance. Always measure from the BASELINE.
Rf is the same for a substance in the same solvent — useful for identification.
One spot doesn't always mean pure — two substances might have the same Rf.
commonMistakes: Measuring Rf from the top instead of from the baseline.
Saying one Rf value proves identity — need to test in multiple solvents.

Identifying Substances.intro: Chemists use a range of tests to identify unknown elements, ions and compounds. Flame tests and gas tests are the most common examples at GCSE.

sections.title: Flame Tests
points: Lithium (Li⁺) — crimson/red
Sodium (Na⁺) — yellow/orange
Potassium (K⁺) — lilac/purple
Calcium (Ca²⁺) — orange-red
Copper (Cu²⁺) — green/blue-green

sections.title: Gas Tests
points: Hydrogen — lit splint → squeaky pop
Oxygen — glowing splint → relights
Carbon dioxide — limewater → turns cloudy (milky)
Chlorine — damp litmus paper → turns white (bleaches)

sections.title: Ion Tests
points: Carbonate (CO₃²⁻): add dilute acid → fizzes (CO₂ produced)
Sulfate (SO₄²⁻): add dilute HCl then BaCl₂ → white precipitate
Halides: add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃ → white (Cl⁻), cream (Br⁻), yellow (I⁻) precipitate

keyTerms.def: Test identifying metal ions by the colour produced in a flame
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed
Calcium hydroxide solution — turns cloudy in presence of CO₂

examTips: Sodium gives a very intense yellow flame — can mask other ions in a mixture.
Oxygen = glowing splint relights. Hydrogen = lit splint squeaky pop. Don't mix these up.
For sulfate test: add HCl FIRST to remove any carbonate ions, THEN add BaCl₂.
commonMistakes: Confusing hydrogen (squeaky pop) with oxygen (relights glowing splint).
Saying calcium is yellow — sodium is yellow; calcium is orange-red.
